Even though a small, rational part of me knows the house is empty and it sounds impossible, the terror and guilt feel absolute. It's only on those rare days when the heavy despair lifts slightly that the certainty and the voice finally fade into the background.\n\nDoctor: Can you think of any situation or evidence that could potentially change your mind about being responsible for your husband's death and the voice you hear being real?\n\nPatient: To be honest, I can't think of anything that would change my mind, even though my daughter and the doctors keep telling me it's not my fault. When I am in that dark place, the guilt and his voice feel completely real and unshakeable to me. It's only on those rare days when the heavy sadness lifts slightly that the certainty of my guilt and the voice feel a bit more distant.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever experienced any other delusions or firmly held beliefs that you know are not true, aside from the belief that you caused your husband's death and the voice you hear?\n\nPatient: No, I’ve never experienced anything else like this. Before his passing, I never experienced anything like this, so when my mood is lighter, I can start to see that these overwhelming feelings and voices might be tied to my grief rather than being the absolute, factual reality."

When the depression feels a bit lighter, the voice and the certainty of being punished also fade into the background.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how you differentiate between the voice you hear and your own thoughts, and do you think the voice is trying to communicate something specific to you or is it just accusatory?\n\nPatient: The voice sounds completely external and clear as day, like someone is physically in the room speaking to me, which is how I tell it apart from my own thoughts. The only time they ever fade a little is on those rare days when the heavy sadness itself lifts slightly.\n\nDoctor: Do you believe that these thoughts of guilt and the voice you hear are realistic, or do you think they might be an exaggerated or distorted way of thinking about yourself and your role in your husband's death?\n\nPatient: I know it probably sounds irrational to others, especially since I know I'm physically alone in the house, but I still feel an unshakeable, terrifying certainty that the voice and my guilt are real. I just feel constantly exhausted by it.\n\nDoctor: Do you often find yourself thinking that you could have done something to prevent your husband's death or feeling guilty about something related to his passing?\n\nPatient: Yes, I am completely convinced that I caused his heart attack because I ignored all the subtle signs of his illness and failed to get him the medical care he needed. I constantly replay my past mistakes, and I truly believe God is punishing me for being such a selfish wife. It feels like I deserve to be punished for ruining our lives.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how these feelings of guilt and belief that you're being punished affect your daily life and interactions with others, and do you feel like you're able to experience any moments of happiness or relief from these thoughts?\n\nPatient: The guilt has made me completely pull away from my friends, miss deadlines at work, and let basic things like cooking and cleaning completely slide. I feel totally flat and can't find joy in anything, though on the rare days when the heavy sadness lifts even a little, the intense guilt and the voice telling me it's my fault fade into the background a bit too.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me more about what you mean by 'the voice telling me it's my fault' and whether you hear this as an actual voice or more of a thought in your head?\n\nPatient: Yes, it sounds like an actual voice outside my head, especially late at night when the house is quiet. I hear my husband's voice clear as day calling my name or saying, \"This is your fault.\" It leaves me completely terrified because I know I am alone in the house.\n\nDoctor: Have you experienced any other unusual perceptions, such as seeing things that aren't there or feeling like someone is watching you, in addition to hearing your husband's voice?\n\nPatient: No, I haven't seen anything unusual or felt like I was being watched. It's really just the sound of his voice calling my name or blaming me when the house is quiet.\n\nDoctor: Have you experienced any periods where these voices or feelings of guilt were not present, or have they been constant since they started?\n\nPatient: I never experienced these voices or this intense guilt before my husband passed away, but they have been with me almost constantly for over a year now. The only time they ever fade a little is on those rare days when the heavy sadness itself lifts slightly.\n\nDoctor: Do you believe that these thoughts of guilt and the voice you hear are realistic, or do you think they might be an exaggerated or distorted way of thinking about yourself and your role in your husband's death?\n\nPatient: I know it probably sounds irrational to others, especially since I know I'm physically alone in the house, but I still feel an unshakeable, terrifying certainty that the voice and my guilt are real. No matter what anyone else says to comfort me, I just can't shake the conviction that I am truly to blame for his death.\n\nDoctor: Do you think there's any possibility that your belief about causing your husband's death and the voice you hear could be a product of your grief and sadness, rather than an objective reality?\n\nPatient: I never had these thoughts or heard his voice before he passed away, so they are definitely tied to this deep sadness. On the rare days when the heavy despair lifts even a little, the accusing voice and the certainty that I caused his death seem to fade into the background too. But when it's happening, it still feels incredibly real and terrifying, and I just can't shake the belief.\n\nDoctor: When you're not hearing the voice and the guilt feelings are less intense, do you still believe that you actually caused your husband's death, or do you think it might be your grief and sadness talking?\n\nPatient: On those rare days when the heavy sadness and despair ease up, the accusing voice and the absolute certainty that I caused his heart attack fade into the background too. In those brief moments, I can start to realize that those thoughts might just be tied to my overwhelming grief. But as soon as the darkness returns, the conviction feels completely real again.\n\nDoctor: When the sadness is not overwhelming and the voice is not present, do you think you might be able to consider that your guilt and the voice could be symptoms of your grief rather than factual truths about your role in your husband's death?\n\nPatient: Yes, in those rare, lighter moments, I can sometimes step back and think that maybe it is just the grief making me feel this way. But those moments never last, and as soon as the darkness rolls back in, any doubt disappears and the guilt feels entirely real again.\n\nDoctor: When you are hearing the voice and feeling the intense guilt, do you ever have moments where you question whether these experiences are real or part of your grief, or are you completely convinced of their reality at those times?\n\nPatient: In those moments, I am completely convinced of their reality and simply cannot shake the certainty. Even though a small, rational part of me knows the house is empty and it sounds impossible, the terror and guilt feel absolute. It's only on those rare days when the heavy despair lifts slightly that the certainty and the voice finally fade into the background.\n\nDoctor: Can you think of any situation or evidence that could potentially change your mind about being responsible for your husband's death and the voice you hear being real?\n\nPatient: To be honest, I can't think of anything that would change my mind, even though my daughter and the doctors keep telling me it's not my fault.
